title: Multi-channel transcranial current stimulation (mc-tCS): a novel approach to modulate smooth pursuit eye movement control in healthy individuals and patients with psychotic disorders
summary:
Smooth pursuit (SP) eye movements – when your eyes smoothly follow a moving object – are a great way to study how our brain integrates sensation (i.e., what we see, hear and feel) with how our body moves, including eye movements. People with psychosis often struggle with pursuit eye movements, suggesting issues with their brain's processing. This makes SP deficits a key biomarker for psychosis. The main brain areas involved in SP include V5 (for visual motion processing) and the Frontal Eye Fields (FEF), which generate the eye movement command. Moreover, alterations in occipito-fronto-parietal networks (which include V5) are linked to visual disturbances reported by about 50% of psychosis patients. More severe visual disturbances correlate with poorer functional remission, highlighting the clinical importance of these visual processing networks. However, little is known about temporal dynamics of the SP network both in healthy individuals or psychosis patients. 

We are investigating how the SP network works by observing individual brain activity during SP using electroencephalography (EEG), functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and eye tracking. Furthermore, we will test the causal role of observed brain activity by using transcranial current stimulation (tCS) to modulate brain activity and, consequently, SP eye movements. The application of tCS will be personalized based on individual brain activity and anatomy to improve specificity and efficacy of the tCS. A promising tCS method is transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), which uses different low or high frequencies (e.g., alpha, gamma) to modulate temporal dynamics of brain activity and the connectivity between different brain areas in a network. Prior work showed personalized tACS could alter covert visuo-spatial attention in healthy individuals. Given the overlap between attention and eye movement brain networks, tACS might also affect SP eye movements and the associated brain activity. tACS targeting area V5 may also modulate its downstream connections, affecting sensorimotor integration during SP and the deficits in SP and clinical measures in psychosis patients. Our overarching study goal is to improve tCS protocols, based on understanding the SP network and improve altered brain activity and SP in psychosis, for clinical use.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- IQ above 70
- sufficient visual acuity (0.8 – 1.0)
- fluent German language
- written informed consent for participation in the study
- Psychosis patients: schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder according to ICD-10 criteria
Exclusion criteria:
- substance abuse during the last three months or lifetime substance dependence
- intake of sedative or other medication with known oculomotor effects 48 hours prior to testing (benzodiazepines, carbamazepine)
- history of severe head trauma or brain damage including stroke, tumor, epilepsy
